name: Raw meat / raw liver diet

chain: More growth, better skin and bones
angle.text: Some forum members eat raw meat, organs and dairy expecting more natural IGF-1 and growth hormone, better skin and stronger development. The expected benefits come from anecdote and theory; no human trials have tested the diet for appearance outcomes.

summary: Eating uncooked meat and organs for supposed growth-factor, skin and bone gains; no human trials exist, and documented infections are tied to raw liver and undercooked meat.
note: Case reports and reviews link raw liver and undercooked meat to parasitic and viral infections.
currentQuick:
The raw meat or raw liver diet is a variant of meat-based eating in which animal foods, including organs such as liver and heart, are eaten uncooked. On looksmax.org it is promoted by some members for supposed growth hormone and IGF-1 effects and skin or body benefits, and criticized by others.
No published human studies have tested it for appearance outcomes. The medical literature in this area is mostly case reports and reviews describing infections linked to raw liver and undercooked meat.
How it works: Proponents say raw animal foods retain nutrients that cooking degrades and boost natural IGF-1 and growth hormone production. No clinical study has tested these claims. Raw liver is a rich source of vitamins and minerals including preformed vitamin A.
Risks and caveats: Reviews and case reports link raw liver to Taenia asiatica tapeworm infection, fascioliasis, toxoplasmosis, toxocariasis and halzoun syndrome, and undercooked pork products to hepatitis E. Wikipedia reports that a single slice of beef liver can exceed the tolerable upper intake for preformed vitamin A, and that thorough cooking kills parasites, viruses and most bacteria.
deepLead:
The raw meat or raw liver diet involves eating meat, organs and often dairy uncooked. One looksmax.org member describing his plan listed raw milk products, raw organs such as liver, hearts and bones, raw meat and fish, and occasional fruit with no vegetables, citing natural IGF-1 production, increased growth hormone and skin endurance as expected benefits. 
Other members argue the approach is hype from TikTok and could affect health during puberty.  No published trials have examined raw meat or raw liver diets in people for appearance or health outcomes.
The medical literature documents infections tied to raw liver and undercooked meat, including tapeworm in Taiwanese communities that ate raw wild boar liver, toxoplasmosis outbreaks in Korea after raw pig liver or spleen, and halzoun syndrome from raw sheep liver in the Eastern Mediterranean.  Wikipedia reports that thorough cooking kills parasites, viruses and most bacteria.

name: Raw milk

chain: Claimed growth, skin and digestion gains
angle.text: In primal and carnivore-style circles raw milk is discussed for height in adolescents, skin, digestion and hormones. Reviews of nutrient content find little difference from pasteurized milk, and the appearance claims rest on anecdote.

summary: Unpasteurized milk, pushed in some circles for height, skin and 'primal' health; reviews find little nutritional gain from skipping pasteurization and documented infection risks.
note: Health agencies document outbreaks of Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter linked to raw milk; sale is restricted or banned in many places.
currentQuick:
Raw milk is milk that has not been heated (pasteurized) to kill microbes. In looksmaxxing and 'primal diet' circles it is promoted as a more nutrient-dense, enzyme-rich food that some say supports skin, hormones, digestion and, for the young, height.
A 2011 systematic review found that pasteurization changes some vitamin levels slightly and that its effect on nutritive value is minimal, and it found no good evidence for claims about allergy, cancer or lactose intolerance. Other forum members argue that raw milk cannot change bone structure after growth plates fuse, and some call the practice 'cope'.
How it works: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes, immunoglobulins, vitamins and beneficial bacteria, so unheated milk keeps more of them active. Pasteurization is designed to reduce viable pathogens; the review literature reports measurable reductions in some water-soluble vitamins (B1, B2, C, folate) but small overall nutritional effect.
Risks and caveats: Raw milk can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter, and pregnant women, children, older adults and immunocompromised people are at greatest risk of serious illness. Legal status varies: some places ban retail sale, others allow farm sales with labels. Forum members also report acne or bloating, and some discuss large intakes for body-composition goals.
deepLead:
Raw milk, also called unpasteurized milk, is milk from cows, goats, sheep or other animals that has not been heat-treated to reduce microbes. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as part of 'primal' or carnivore-style eating, with claims about skin, digestion, hormones and, for adolescents, height.
A 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies found that pasteurization lowered vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, raised or left others unchanged, and had minimal effect on the milk's overall nutritive value; it also found no sound evidence that raw milk prevents or treats allergies, cancer or lactose intolerance. A small randomized pilot study on lactose intolerance did not find that raw milk was better tolerated than pasteurized milk.
Public-health literature links raw milk to infections including listeriosis, brucellosis, salmonellosis and tick-borne encephalitis, and describes its microbiota as a mix of beneficial, spoilage and pathogenic organisms. Rules differ widely by country and US state.

name: Seed oil avoidance

angle.text: Followers exclude canola, soybean, sunflower and similar oils in the belief they drive inflammation that shows up as skin problems, puffiness and body fat. It is bundled with other clean-eating ideas in looksmaxxing forums; nutrition reviews generally have not supported the harm claims.

summary: Cutting canola, soybean, sunflower and similar oils for skin and health; popular online, while nutrition reviews generally do not support the harm claims.
note: No trials were found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or looks; major reviews of dietary evidence do not support the harm claims.
currentQuick:
Seed oil avoidance means removing refined vegetable oils such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn and safflower from the diet and cooking with fats like butter, tallow or olive oil. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to improve skin, inflammation and general health, often alongside carnivore or primal eating.
Nutrition reviews and health bodies generally report that these oils do not reliably raise inflammation and that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is associated with better cardiovascular markers. No clinical studies were found that test seed oil avoidance for appearance.
How it works: Proponents point to omega-6 linoleic acid (said to promote inflammation), a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio, and industrial solvent extraction as reasons for harm. Researchers say trials do not show linoleic acid reliably raising inflammatory markers and that absolute intake, not the ratio, should guide advice.
Risks and caveats: Avoiding seed oils is not itself documented as harmful, but reviews note that shifting toward saturated fat could raise LDL cholesterol. Forum users also note it is hard to avoid oils in restaurants, and some posters acknowledge that the effect size is unclear.
deepLead:
Seed oil avoidance is a dietary practice in which people exclude refined oils pressed or solvent-extracted from seeds, such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn, cottonseed, safflower, grapeseed and rice bran, often called the 'hateful eight' in online discussion. Adherents say the oils drive inflammation, skin problems and chronic disease; in looksmaxxing forums it is bundled with other 'clean' eating ideas.
Reviews of human evidence report that linoleic acid, the main omega-6 fat in these oils, does not reliably raise inflammatory markers, and that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is linked to better cardiovascular risk markers. A 2025 narrative review describes the campaign against seed oils as contrary to dietary guidelines and available human research. No clinical studies were found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or facial appearance.

name: Fasting for face fat

chain: Calorie intake and body fat fall
angle.text: Users adopt intermittent fasting such as time-restricted eating or 5:2 to lower body fat and slim the face as part of cutting and hollow-cheek aesthetics. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie reduction; facial fat has not been tested specifically.

summary: Intermittent fasting used to slim the face; trials show weight loss similar to ordinary calorie cutting, but nothing tests facial fat specifically.
note: No study has measured facial fat loss from fasting; fat loss sites are not chosen by the dieter, and health bodies advise against fasting for several groups.
currentQuick:
Fasting for face fat means using intermittent fasting (eating only in a window, alternate days, or occasional whole-day fasts) to lose body fat and, forum members hope, reveal a leaner face. It is discussed alongside cutting and 'leanmaxxing'.
Randomized trials and network meta-analyses show intermittent fasting can produce weight loss roughly comparable to continuous calorie restriction. No trial was found that measures facial fat, and forum members themselves disagree about hormonal downsides.
How it works: Fasting regimens reduce calorie intake and prolong overnight fasting intervals; reviews propose effects via circadian biology, gut microbiome and sleep. How fat is lost from different body regions varies by person and genetics, and forum posters report people with low body fat but fuller faces.
Risks and caveats: Short-term hunger, irritability, dizziness and headache are reported; fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, underweight people or those prone to eating disorders. Forum members worry about effects on testosterone, thyroid and muscle, while a 2025 Cell study reported that intermittent fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration.
deepLead:
Fasting for face fat is the use of intermittent fasting patterns, such as daily time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting or 5:2 schedules, with the aim of lowering body fat and thereby slimming the face. It sits within looksmaxxing discussions of cutting, 'leanmaxxing' and hollow-cheek aesthetics.
A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials in 6,582 adults compared intermittent fasting with continuous energy restriction and unrestricted eating for body weight and cardiometabolic outcomes. Reviews generally describe weight loss similar to ordinary calorie restriction, and the American Heart Association and National Institute on Aging have described evidence for broader benefits as limited. No study has measured facial fat after fasting.

name: Extreme dieting / low body fat

angle.text: Called leanmaxxing, this means cutting to roughly 10 to 15% body fat for facial definition and visible muscle. Forum members disagree on the ideal level and note that facial fat distribution is partly genetic. Sports medicine documents the practice in competition prep.

summary: Cutting to very low body fat for a defined face and physique; sports medicine documents short-term competition practice and health risks of prolonged energy deficit.
note: Prolonged low energy availability is associated with hormonal, bone and mood problems; forum members disagree on how lean is ideal for the face.
currentQuick:
Extreme dieting for low body fat means sustained calorie deficits to reach very lean levels, often discussed on forums in terms of 'hollow cheeks', visible abs and a sharper jaw. Opinions differ: some posters say 10 to 12% body fat is ideal, others say under 12 to 15% is 'cope', and some report their face stayed full even when lean.
Sports-science reviews describe how bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet for competition and note higher protein intakes are recommended during deficits. Expert bodies such as the IOC describe health risks of low energy availability in athletes.
How it works: A sustained energy deficit reduces fat stores across the body. Where fat is lost first varies by person; forum posters report cases with low body fat and a fuller face, which they attribute to genetics. Competitors in physique sports typically hold extreme leanness only for the contest period.
Risks and caveats: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) describes hormonal, bone, mood and performance problems from low energy availability in men and women. Men may have lower androgen levels, bone density and strength. Disordered eating is a recognised concern in weight-sensitive sports.
deepLead:
Extreme dieting to low body fat refers to prolonged or aggressive calorie restriction aimed at reaching very lean physiques, discussed in looksmaxxing communities as 'leanmaxxing' for facial definition and visible muscle. Typical forum targets range from about 10 to 15% body fat, with disagreement about whether leaner is better for the face.
Sports-science literature describes how competitive bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet before events, including peak-week manipulation, and reviews suggest higher protein intakes during caloric restriction in lean resistance-trained athletes. The IOC and the RED-S literature document health risks of low energy availability. No studies have tested extreme leanness specifically for facial appearance.

name: Tapeworm diet

angle.text: The tapeworm diet is an old fad-diet story in which swallowing a tapeworm is meant to produce weight loss and a leaner look. Wikipedia describes it among 19th-century diet hoaxes; medical sources describe infection as a disease, and no appearance studies exist.

summary: Swallowing tapeworms to lose weight, an old fad-diet story; medical sources describe tapeworm infection as a disease with serious risks.
note: Tapeworm infection can cause serious illness, including cysticercosis; no clinical studies support it as a weight-loss method.
currentQuick:
The tapeworm diet is a long-standing diet legend in which a person deliberately swallows a tapeworm so that it absorbs food in the intestine, then takes an anti-parasitic drug once the goal weight is reached. Wikipedia lists it among 19th-century diet hoaxes.
The sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of it and no forum material connecting it to looksmaxxing; it is included here as a weight-loss practice that appears in discussions of extreme diets.
How it works: The claimed idea is that the worm competes with the host for nutrients. Medical sources describe taeniasis as often causing mild or no symptoms, with occasional weight loss as a symptom of infection rather than a method.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes risk of gastric obstruction in the diet story, and its tapeworm article describes more serious infections: cysticercosis from Taenia solium eggs can reach the brain, eyes and muscles, and the fish tapeworm can cause pernicious anemia through B12 absorption.
deepLead:
The tapeworm diet is a purported weight-loss method in which a person swallows a tapeworm or its eggs so the parasite absorbs part of the food eaten, then ends it with an anti-parasitic medicine. Wikipedia describes it among 19th-century 'diet hoaxes', with no specific year given.
Medical descriptions treat tapeworm infection as a disease. Taeniasis, intestinal infection with adult Taenia worms, is usually acquired from undercooked beef or pork, often causes few or mild symptoms and only occasionally weight loss, while cysticercosis from swallowing T. solium eggs can cause serious or fatal damage to the brain, eyes and other tissues. No clinical studies of tapeworm ingestion as a weight-loss method were found.

name: Cold showers

angle.text: Users take cold showers for claimed benefits to skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline. Meta-analyses find mood and stress effects of uncertain strength; the skin, hair and hormone claims are based on anecdote.

summary: Cold-water exposure for skin, hair, mood and testosterone claims; meta-analyses find mood and stress signals of uncertain strength, with nothing solid on looks.
note: Cold immersion can trigger cardiac and breathing responses; health bodies advise caution, and the Wim Hof breathing component has been linked to blackout deaths.
currentQuick:
Cold showers are showers at low water temperature, adopted in forums for claimed benefits to skin, hair, mood, discipline and hormones. Posts range from enthusiastic ('my skin is better, my hair is better') to critical (that cold showers worsen eye bags or make features look harsher).
Systematic reviews of cold-water exposure report pooled signals toward better mood, perceived stress and wellbeing, but with wide confidence intervals, small studies and attenuated results in controlled-only analyses. No study was found testing cold showers for skin appearance or testosterone.
How it works: Cold exposure triggers the cold shock response, vasoconstriction and a sympathetic nervous system surge. Repeated cold showers have been shown to reduce the initial responses to later cold-water immersion. Proponents propose hormetic stress and mood effects; for skin and hair, forum claims about circulation and oil are untested.
Risks and caveats: Cold-water immersion can cause gasping, heart rate and blood pressure surges, and arrhythmias in some people. Wikipedia reports that the American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy. Combining breath-holding or hyperventilation with water is linked to blackout and drowning reports.
deepLead:
Cold showers are showers taken with cold water, used in looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities for claimed effects on skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline. The practice overlaps with ice baths, cold plunges and the Wim Hof Method.
A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of cold-water immersion in healthy adults assessed outcomes including sleep, stress, fatigue, skin health, immunity, mood and anxiety, and a 2026 meta-analysis of 13 studies found pooled estimates generally favoured cold-water exposure for depressive symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, but with wide confidence intervals and attenuated results in controlled-only analyses. No study was found testing cold showers for testosterone or facial appearance.

name: Cold plunge / face ice dunk

angle.text: Looksmaxxing users dunk the face in ice water mainly to reduce morning puffiness and tighten the look of the skin. Whole-body cold plunges are linked more to recovery. The facial routine is popular on forums, with no published trials on it.

summary: Dunking the face (or whole body) in ice water, mainly to reduce morning puffiness; popular on forums, with no published trials on the facial use.
note: Full-body cold immersion carries documented cardiac and cold-shock risks; no trials test face dunking for appearance.
currentQuick:
A face ice dunk means submerging the face in a bowl of ice water for a short time, usually with the stated aim of reducing facial puffiness or swelling. A cold plunge is the whole-body version, typically in a tub of cold water. Both are discussed in appearance communities as a low-cost routine.
No published human study has tested face dunking for facial depuffing. Related research covers whole-body cold-water immersion for exercise recovery, where reviews describe mixed results, and cold therapy for swelling after injury, where reviews also describe inconclusive findings.
How it works: Cold causes blood vessels near the skin to constrict and lowers local metabolic activity, which proponents say reduces fluid pooling and swelling. Reference sources describe vasoconstriction and reduced local inflammation as effects of cold exposure, while noting the internal processes are not fully understood.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources list cold shock response, cardiac stress, hypothermia and frostbite or cold burns as documented risks of cold exposure, mostly in the context of whole-body immersion; one British death during cold-water therapy was reported in 2022. Cold allergy and circulation disorders are listed contraindications for cold therapy. Face-specific risks are not well studied.
deepLead:
A cold plunge or ice dunk is a routine in which the body, or in the facial variant only the face, is briefly submerged in cold or ice water. In looksmaxxing communities the face version is mostly discussed as a way to reduce morning facial puffiness. The whole-body version is more widely associated with sports recovery and wellness culture, where it is also known as an ice bath or cold-water immersion.
No published clinical study has examined face ice dunking for puffiness or any other appearance outcome. Research on whole-body cold-water immersion concerns mainly exercise recovery, and its findings are described as mixed. Medical sources on cold therapy for swelling after injury or surgery also describe the evidence as mixed or inconclusive.

name: Sungazing

angle.text: Some users sungaze in the hope of lightening iris color or improving vision. The practice dates to early 20th-century eye exercises. The iris-lightening idea rests on belief and anecdote, and ophthalmology literature documents retinal burns from it.

summary: Staring at the sun for claimed eye, mood and even iris-colour benefits; ophthalmology literature documents retinal burns from it.
note: Ophthalmology reports describe permanent retinal damage (solar retinopathy) from direct sun viewing.
currentQuick:
Sungazing is the practice of looking directly at the sun, usually near sunrise or sunset, for spiritual or health reasons. In looksmaxxing forums, users have discussed it in connection with claims about eyesight, mood, skin and eye colour.
No published trial supports benefits to vision or appearance. Ophthalmology literature, by contrast, contains many case reports and series of solar retinopathy, retinal injury after direct sun viewing.
How it works: Proponents say sunlight entering the eyes affects hormones, circadian rhythm and mood, and some believe it changes iris pigment. Ophthalmology research describes a different mechanism: high-energy visible and ultraviolet light can damage retinal cells photochemically, and the retina has no pain receptors, so injury can go unnoticed.
Risks and caveats: Solar retinopathy typically causes central blind spots, distorted vision and light sensitivity. Many cases recover over weeks to six months, but some produce lasting foveal defects. Reviews and case reports also link repeated bright-light exposure to concerns about macular degeneration.
deepLead:
Sungazing is the practice of looking directly at the sun, often near dawn or dusk, as a spiritual or health practice. A general reference describes it as an unsafe and pseudoscientific practice; it was promoted in the early 20th century by William Horatio Bates under the name sunning, as part of his eye exercises for myopia.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve eyesight, mood, skin or eye colour, with some users posting about their own experiences, including floaters. No published trial has tested these claims. The medical literature instead documents solar retinopathy, a retinal injury following exposure to the sun's light, including from direct sungazing.

name: Urine therapy

angle.text: Followers of urine therapy drink or apply urine, sometimes aged, for rejuvenation and skin. The practice has roots in yoga traditions. The appearance claims rest on tradition and anecdote, with no studies showing a benefit.

summary: Drinking or applying urine for rejuvenation or skin; no evidence of benefit, with documented contamination concerns.
note: Medical sources report no demonstrated benefit and warn of risks; a looksmax.org user reported a negative experience.
currentQuick:
Urine therapy is an alternative-medicine practice in which a person drinks their own urine or applies it to the skin or gums for health or cosmetic purposes. It has traditional roots in several cultures and was popularised in modern times by the British naturopath John W. Armstrong in the 20th century.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a rejuvenation or skin practice, with proponents citing the idea that urine contains beneficial substances. A reference source states there is no scientific evidence of therapeutic benefit from untreated urine.
How it works: Proponents attribute effects to substances in urine, such as urea or claimed stem cells. Urine is over 95 percent water, and commercial urea creams use synthetic urea at concentrations far higher than urine provides.
Risks and caveats: Sources report no demonstrated benefit and note microbial contamination concerns. The American Cancer Society states that evidence does not support urine or urea helping cancer patients. One looksmax.org user posted a report of a negative experience drinking aged urine, describing a burning throat and nausea.
deepLead:
Urine therapy, also called urotherapy, urinotherapy or shivambu, is an alternative-medicine practice that uses human urine for medicinal or cosmetic purposes, including drinking it and massaging it into skin or gums. In medieval hatha yoga a related practice was called amaroli.
Medical and reference sources state there is no scientific evidence supporting claimed therapeutic benefits of untreated urine. In looksmaxxing communities the practice appears mainly as a claimed rejuvenation or skin method, and at least one forum user has posted a first-person report of a negative experience.
The term urotherapy is also used in paediatric urology for non-surgical bladder training and behavioural treatment; that use is unrelated to urine therapy as discussed here.

name: Sunbathing / tanmaxxing

angle.text: Tanmaxxing means darkening the skin with sun, lamps, tanning lotions or sunless products for a healthier, more attractive complexion. The color change is immediately visible. Tanning is the skin's pigment response to ultraviolet radiation.

summary: Getting a tan with sun, lamps or sunless products for a healthier-looking complexion; tans are a documented skin-damage response.
note: WHO, the American Cancer Society and the US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning; sunless tanning products avoid UV.
currentQuick:
Tanmaxxing is the community term for tanning to improve how the skin looks, whether by sunbathing, tanning products or sunless alternatives. Tanned skin has been fashionable in the West since the 1920s, and looksmaxxing guides treat colour as part of skin and overall appearance.
Research on UV exposure documents an association with sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer, and expert guidance generally cautions against UV tanning. Sunless self-tanners using dihydroxyacetone are described as a way to darken skin without UV.
How it works: UV radiation prompts melanocytes to make melanin. UVA darkens existing pigment through oxidative stress, while UVB causes DNA damage that triggers new melanin production and a tan that appears a few days later. Sunless tanners react with proteins in the outer skin layer to produce a brown colour.
Risks and caveats: Excess UV is associated with sunburn, DNA mutations, skin cancer, accelerated skin ageing and immune suppression. A 2010 study linked frequent tanning bed use to about triple the melanoma risk. Skin type matters: people with fair skin burn more easily.
deepLead:
Tanmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for darkening the skin, by sunbathing, tanning oils and lotions, tanning devices or sunless products, to look healthier or more attractive. Tanning itself is the skin's pigment response to ultraviolet radiation.
Research and public-health bodies document that UV exposure is associated with sunburn, skin ageing and skin cancer, and organisations including the WHO, the American Cancer Society and the US Surgeon General warn against excessive sun and indoor tanning exposure. Sun exposure also supports vitamin D production. Sunless products based on dihydroxyacetone darken the skin without UV.

name: Sleepmaxxing

angle.text: Users optimise sleep with darkness, routines, blue-light blocking and sometimes supplements or peptides, aiming for brighter skin, fewer dark circles and better recovery. Sleep hygiene has weak-to-mixed trial support for insomnia; effects on looks specifically are untested.

summary: Optimising sleep for looks and energy, from darkness and routines to supplements and peptides; sleep hygiene has weak-to-mixed trial support alone.
note: The AASM advises against sleep hygiene as stand-alone chronic insomnia therapy; forum threads also discuss unapproved peptides.
currentQuick:
Sleepmaxxing is the looksmaxxing and wellness term for optimising sleep, typically through a dark, cool, quiet bedroom, a fixed schedule, limiting evening light and food, and sometimes products such as blue-light-blocking glasses or supplements.
Much of it overlaps with sleep hygiene, a set of behavioural recommendations developed in the late 1970s. A 2014 review described evidence that sleep hygiene improves sleep as weak and inconclusive, although some individual items have stronger support.
How it works: Proponents say regular timing and darkness steady the circadian rhythm, which they link to melatonin production, sleep quality and next-day appearance and energy. Sleep hygiene research describes behavioural and environmental factors, such as noise, alcohol and mental activity before bed, as influencing sleep.
Risks and caveats: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine concluded in 2021 that sleep hygiene should not be used alone as a therapy for chronic insomnia, warning it could delay effective treatment. A forum guide notes that sleep medication can lose effect with daily use and that melatonin may disturb the circadian rhythm if taken daily; forum threads also discuss research peptides.
deepLead:
Sleepmaxxing is a social-media and looksmaxxing term for optimising sleep. Most of the content overlaps with sleep hygiene, a set of behavioural and environmental practices developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia. Coverage of the sleepmaxxing trend has appeared in Time and The Guardian in 2025.
On looksmax.org, threads describe routines involving blue-light avoidance, a dark room, cooling bedding and sunrise lamps, plus supplements and peptides. Systematic review evidence that sleep hygiene improves sleep is described as weak and inconclusive, and a 2021 AASM paper advised against it as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.

name: Smellmaxxing

angle.text: Smellmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for managing body scent with hygiene, deodorant and fragrance as part of overall attractiveness. It is a minor topic. Body-odour science exists, though there is little published on the looksmaxxing claims.

summary: Optimising body scent as part of attractiveness; the body-odour science is real but sparse on looksmaxxing claims.
note: Thin source base; research on body odour and attraction exists but nothing tests the looksmaxxing framing.
currentQuick:
Smellmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for improving how one smells, through hygiene, deodorant, diet or fragrance, on the idea that scent contributes to attractiveness. A forum thread has asked whether good smell can compensate for looks.
Body odour science is better developed than the slang. Research describes how skin bacteria acting on gland secretions create odour, and some studies examine scent and partner preference, though findings are limited in scope.
How it works: Most body odour comes from bacterial activity on secretions of apocrine glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits. Genetics (notably the ABCC11 gene) and diet also affect odour. Deodorants reduce odour, while antiperspirants block sweat pores temporarily.
Risks and caveats: No notable harms are documented for ordinary hygiene or fragrance use in the sources reviewed. Studies on scent and attraction are small and do not establish how much scent affects perceived attractiveness.
deepLead:
Smellmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for optimising body scent as part of overall attractiveness. It is a minor topic in appearance communities and the available published source material on the term itself is thin.
Reference material on body odour states that the main contribution comes from bacterial activity on skin gland secretions, with diet, sex, health and medication also playing roles. Studies discussed in the same reference report that women tend to prefer the scent of men whose immune genes differ from their own, and that fruit and vegetable intake was linked to sweat described as more pleasant.

name: Gymmaxxing

angle.text: Gymmaxxing is lifting and leaning out for looks, usually emphasising leanness and shoulder width. Muscle-building physiology is well described; the effect on attractiveness specifically is untested. Some forum members argue lifting cannot offset facial flaws.

summary: Lifting and leaning out for looks: the physiology of muscle gain is well described, but its effect on attractiveness is untested.
note: Training science is established; whether it changes attractiveness is debated and unstudied here.
currentQuick:
Gymmaxxing means resistance training and eating to build muscle and reduce body fat in order to look better. It is one of the most commonly recommended softmaxxes in looksmaxxing communities.
The underlying exercise science is well established, while claims about how much it improves attractiveness or dating outcomes rest on forum anecdotes and have not been tested directly.
How it works: Resistance training places mechanical tension on muscle, which activates growth signalling, and results depend on training volume, progressive overload, nutrition and individual genetics, according to general descriptions of hypertrophy.
Risks and caveats: Training carries ordinary injury risks, and forum guides warn about ego lifting and poor form. Forum threads also discuss anabolic steroids alongside gymmaxxing, a separate topic with documented medical risks.
deepLead:
Gymmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for resistance training and related fitness practices pursued to improve physical appearance and attractiveness, usually by building muscle and lowering body fat. Wikipedia lists exercise among the non-invasive, softmaxxing-type practices in looksmaxxing culture , and a Grokipedia entry on looksmaxxing describes fitness as a core lever, with an emphasis on leanness and shoulder width rather than extreme muscle mass .
On forums such as looksmax.org, users write long guides on training theory, post before-and-after transformation photos and debate whether lifting changes how attractive a person is when facial features are held constant . Guides commonly cite mechanical tension, progressive overload and training volume, concepts that also appear in general descriptions of muscle hypertrophy .
Exercise science supports the physiological premise that resistance training increases muscle size . No published study found for this entry has tested gymmaxxing as a looksmaxxing strategy, so its effect on rated attractiveness or dating outcomes is untested; the forum debate over how much it helps is unresolved .

name: Alcohol/sugar/dairy face avoidance

angle.text: Users drop alcohol, added sugar and dairy hoping for a less puffy, clearer, leaner face. Related acne and hydration research exists; facial leanness itself has not been tested for these changes.

summary: Dropping alcohol, sugar and dairy for a leaner face: related acne and hydration research exists, but facial leanness itself is untested.
note: Evidence comes from acne, rosacea and sleep research, not from studies of facial appearance.
currentQuick:
This practice involves avoiding alcohol, added sugar and dairy in the belief that it makes the face look leaner, less puffy or clearer. It is discussed as a diet-side softmaxx, often alongside fat loss.
No study has tested the combination for facial appearance. Related research covers acne and glycemic load, weak links between milk and acne, and alcohol's effects on hydration, sleep and flushing.
How it works: Proposed routes are lower body fat, less fluid retention, better sleep and fewer acne flares. Wikipedia describes insulin and IGF-1 pathways for sugar and dairy in acne, and diuretic and sleep-disrupting effects for alcohol.
Risks and caveats: Removing foods is generally low risk, but very restrictive diets can cause nutritional shortfalls, and Grokipedia notes severe dieting practices carry health risks.
deepLead:
Alcohol, sugar and dairy face avoidance refers to the idea, discussed in appearance-focused communities, that cutting alcohol, added sugar and dairy from the diet produces a leaner-looking, less puffy or clearer face. It is a dietary variant of softmaxxing, the group of non-invasive practices in looksmaxxing that includes skincare, grooming and weight management .
Research on the three foods differs. Wikipedia reports that trials and observational work link high-glycemic-load diets with acne and that dermatologists recommend diets low in simple sugars, while evidence tying milk to acne is described as weak and observational . Alcohol is described as a diuretic that disrupts sleep, and it is listed as a flushing trigger in rosacea .
No published trial found for this entry has tested removing all three foods together for facial appearance, and facial leanness or puffiness has not been measured as an outcome. Evidence is therefore limited to related research on acne, rosacea, hydration and sleep.

name: Softmaxxing

angle.text: Softmaxxing is the non-invasive end of looksmaxxing: skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture and weight management. Forum guides describe it as low-risk and reversible. The label itself has not been tested, though many component habits are visibly effective.

summary: The non-invasive end of looksmaxxing (skincare, grooming, sleep, fitness): low risk, but the label itself has never been tested.
note: Evidence differs by component; claims like '50-70% of potential' are uncited forum figures.
currentQuick:
Softmaxxing is the looksmaxxing name for reversible, low-risk practices such as skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture, sleep and exercise. It is set against hardmaxxing, which covers surgery and drugs.
Forum guides present it as the starting point, but no study has tested softmaxxing as a whole. Its components have separate evidence bases, mostly from dermatology and general health guidance.
How it works: Practitioners improve skin quality, grooming and presentation, and body composition, and some add practices such as mewing that have little scientific support according to Grokipedia.
Risks and caveats: Most components are low risk. Researchers have noted that online skincare content mixes commercial claims with advice and can encourage irritating self-experimentation, and critics link looksmaxxing culture generally to body-image distress.
deepLead:
Softmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for non-invasive appearance improvements such as skincare, haircuts, grooming, clothing, posture, weight management and exercise. It is contrasted with hardmaxxing, which covers surgery, drugs and other invasive or extreme methods . A looksmax.org guide defines it as non-invasive, reversible, low-risk improvements that raise attractiveness without surgery or medical intervention .
Wikipedia also places less conventional practices such as mewing and NoFap under the softmaxxing heading , while Grokipedia describes basics such as twice-daily cleansing, daily sunscreen, oral hygiene and good posture and notes that mewing has little scientific support . Forum users commonly advise doing softmaxxes before considering hardmaxxing .
No clinical trials of softmaxxing as a package were found. Research touching the area includes a 2026 narrative review of digital skincare content and acne treatment adherence  and a 2026 cross-sectional analysis of online discourse on looksmaxxing, softmaxxing and hardmaxxing . Individual components such as skincare and exercise have their own, separate evidence bases.

name: Body dysmorphia & mirror checking

angle.text: Body dysmorphic disorder and mirror checking come up in looksmaxxing communities as the mental-health side of appearance focus. It is a recognised psychiatric condition marked by preoccupation with minor perceived flaws, which clinicians treat with CBT and SSRIs.

summary: Compulsive checking and appearance fixation: a recognised psychiatric condition (BDD) that clinicians say CBT and SSRIs can treat.
note: Reviews report high rates of suicidal ideation in BDD; resources exist through mental health professionals.
currentQuick:
Body dysmorphic disorder is a psychiatric condition in which a person spends hours on perceived flaws in their appearance that others barely notice. Mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflage are typical behaviours, and some people avoid mirrors instead.
Looksmaxxing communities involve heavy self-scrutiny, and critics cited by Wikipedia link the culture to body dysmorphia. No controlled study found establishes how often BDD occurs in these communities.
How it works: Clinical models treat checking and similar safety behaviours as maintaining appearance concern. Treatment research focuses on cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and ritual prevention, and on serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report significant impairment, frequent comorbid depression and anxiety, and relatively common suicidal ideation. Cosmetic treatment typically does not relieve the distress, according to Wikipedia, and BDD is often underdiagnosed.
deepLead:
Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a psychiatric condition marked by persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance that are minor or unnoticeable to others, together with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflaging . Mirror checking, along with its opposite, mirror avoidance, is among the best-described of these behaviours .
In looksmaxxing communities, appearance scrutiny, self-rating and photo comparison are routine, and journalists and researchers have discussed whether these habits overlap with or worsen body dysmorphia. Wikipedia reports that critics describe looksmaxxing as linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation ; Grokipedia likewise says self-rating and comparison are linked to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety . The articles do not present controlled studies establishing that looksmaxxing causes BDD.
Clinical reviews describe cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors as the best-supported treatments . Reviews also report that people with BDD frequently seek cosmetic or dermatological treatment and that BDD is common in those settings .

name: Subliminals for appearance

angle.text: Listeners play subliminal audio hoping to grow taller, change eye color, improve jaw growth or reduce hair loss through the subconscious. No study has tested physical change from these recordings, and forum members are themselves split, with some attributing effects to expectation.

summary: Audio tracks claimed to reshape the body via the subconscious: no study has tested physical change, and forum members themselves are split.
note: No published studies on physical appearance; related research concerns psychological outcomes.
currentQuick:
Appearance subliminals are audio recordings that supposedly deliver hidden messages to change features such as height, eye colour or jaw growth. They circulate on looksmaxxing forums and on subreddits dedicated to the practice.
No study has tested them for physical change. Subliminal-perception research mostly finds limited effects on behaviour a person already intends, and one self-concept trial found effects resembling placebo apart from a self-concept change.
How it works: Believers say the subconscious mind can be influenced by sub-audible affirmations. Researchers describe subliminal stimuli as stimuli below conscious perception with limited, context-dependent effects.
Risks and caveats: Direct physical risk is low. Wikipedia notes subliminal advertising is prohibited in several countries.
deepLead:
Subliminal audio, in the form used by looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, consists of recordings that supposedly carry affirmations or intentions below the threshold of conscious hearing, often layered under music or sound, and are listened to in the hope of changing the body, such as growing taller, changing eye colour, improving jaw growth or reducing hair loss . Listeners claim these recordings work by influencing the subconscious mind.
Wikipedia defines subliminal stimuli as sensory stimuli below an individual's threshold for conscious perception, including audio played below audible volume or masked by other sounds . Laboratory research has found effects of such stimuli on brain activity and on actions a person already intends to take, but the American Psychological Association was reported in 2009 as saying there was no conclusive evidence that effects are truly subliminal .
No study found has tested subliminal audio for changing physical appearance. Forum threads show a mix of users reporting results, users citing placebo, and users who say the idea does not work .

name: Colloidal silver

angle.text: Colloidal silver is promoted in alternative-health circles as a supplement and immune aid, and appears in appearance forums in eye color discussions. Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports the health claims; chronic use can cause blue-grey skin (argyria).

summary: Ingested silver suspension sold as a health supplement; claims are unsupported per Wikipedia and chronic use can cause permanent blue-grey skin (argyria).
note: Argyria is described as permanent once it develops.
currentQuick:
Colloidal silver is a suspension of very small silver particles that some alternative-health sources promote as a supplement to ingest for immunity and illness. It has a long history as an antimicrobial and was registered as a biocide in the US in 1954.
Wikipedia states no medical evidence supports it for the claimed uses, and silver is not an essential mineral. Its most visible documented effect on appearance is argyria, a lasting blue-grey skin colour.
How it works: Silver particles have antimicrobial properties in laboratory and wound-dressing contexts, and are used in medical devices and textiles. Reviews say ingested nanosilver is not inert and distributes to tissues such as the liver.
Risks and caveats: Chronic ingestion or inhalation of silver can cause argyria, which Wikipedia says does not resolve after exposure stops. Reviews report liver and lung effects of inhaled nanosilver in rats, and the US EPA classifies antimicrobial silver nanoparticles as pesticides.
deepLead:
Colloidal silver is a suspension of tiny silver particles in a liquid, historically described as nanosilver when the particles are below 100 nanometres. It is promoted in some alternative-health circles as a dietary supplement to ingest as a health or immune aid . Wikipedia says colloidal silver has been marketed as an essential mineral supplement and as a way to prevent or treat cancer, diabetes, arthritis, HIV/AIDS, herpes and tuberculosis, and states that no medical evidence supports it for these claims .
The best-documented appearance-related effect is argyria, a blue-grey discolouration of skin and other tissues that Wikipedia says can follow chronic ingestion or inhalation of silver, including colloidal silver, and that does not resolve after exposure stops .
Silver in dressings and sinus irrigations has been investigated in laboratory and clinical settings, and reviews state that nanosilver is not inert in the body . No study found has examined ingested colloidal silver for appearance.

name: Eye color change drops

angle.text: Users discuss drops, such as latanoprost-type or homemade ones, to lighten brown eyes toward blue, green or hazel, alongside keratopigmentation and laser depigmentation. No peer-reviewed study has examined a cosmetic drop for this; surgical routes carry documented eye risks.

summary: Eye drops, and the wider set of eye-color procedures, that people hope will lighten brown eyes; drops have no published support and the surgical routes carry documented eye risks.
note: Prescription glaucoma drops such as latanoprost are documented to darken, not lighten, iris color; surgical alternatives have reported vision-threatening complications.
currentQuick:
Eye color change drops refers to the idea, discussed on looksmaxxing forums, that a topical product can lighten the iris. No published human study has tested an over-the-counter or homemade drop for this purpose. The better-documented drug effect runs the other way: the glaucoma medicine latanoprost can increase iris pigment in some people.
In practice the forum conversation is mostly about procedures rather than drops: corneal tattooing (keratopigmentation), laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic iris implants. Review articles describe these as having limited long-term data and, for implants, serious complications.
How it works: Iris color depends largely on the amount of melanin in the iris stroma. Prostaglandin-analogue drops such as latanoprost are reported to raise the melanin content of stromal melanocytes, which darkens the eye. Surgical methods work differently: keratopigmentation places pigment in the cornea, laser depigmentation uses a Nd:YAG laser to remove stromal melanin, and implants cover the iris with a colored artificial disc.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report that cosmetic iris implants are not approved by major regulators and have been linked to glaucoma, uveitis, corneal damage and vision loss. Laser depigmentation has limited long-term safety data, and keratopigmentation is described as the most studied option but still lacking long-term cosmetic evidence. Unregulated drops placed in the eye carry the general risk of contamination and infection, a point raised by forum posters themselves.
deepLead:
Eye color change drops is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for eye drops that are claimed to lighten the color of the iris, usually from brown toward blue, green or hazel. No peer-reviewed study has examined a cosmetic drop for lightening eye color. 
The prescription drug most often connected to the topic is latanoprost, a glaucoma medicine whose labelled side effects include increased brown iris pigmentation, meaning it tends to darken rather than lighten eyes. Microscopy studies attribute the change to more melanin inside existing iris melanocytes. 
Forum discussion largely moves from drops to procedures. Published reviews describe three surgical approaches to cosmetic eye color change: iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic keratopigmentation, with the evidence base strongest for the last and weakest for implants' safety.
